context: This prompt requires creating 6 Python scripts for requirement management (requirement_ur_create.py, requirement_ur_modify.py, requirement_ur_delete.py, requirement_tr_create.py, requirement_tr_modify.py, requirement_tr_delete.py) and updating execution instructions to mandate their use. The scripts will enforce safe, deterministic requirement modifications while following the existing framework patterns. Key design decisions need clarification regarding validation strictness, ID collision handling, error messaging, and instruction update scope.

questions.question-text: Should the validation parameter accept only the three values specified (strict|basic|none), or should it also accept boolean values (true/false) for backward compatibility or simplified usage?

options.label: Only accept the three explicit string values: 'strict', 'basic', 'none'
options.pros: Clear semantics, no ambiguity, matches the prompt specification exactly, easier to document and maintain
options.cons: Less flexible for users who might prefer boolean shortcuts, requires users to type full words

options.label: Accept both string values ('strict'|'basic'|'none') and boolean values (true=basic, false=none)
options.pros: More flexible, allows shorthand usage, easier for users who just want on/off behavior
options.cons: Ambiguous what 'true' means (could be strict or basic), adds complexity, not in original spec

options.label: Accept string values plus boolean shortcuts (true=strict, false=none) with basic as default
options.pros: Flexible, true maps to strictest validation which is safer, false maps to no validation
options.cons: Additional complexity, boolean meaning might not be intuitive, deviation from specification

questions.recommendation-rationale: The prompt explicitly specifies 'validation=strict|basic|none' with basic as default. Adding boolean support would deviate from the specification without clear benefit. Three explicit values provide clear semantics and match the framework's pattern of explicit parameter values (like state=active|completed in prompt_create.py).

questions.question-text: When creating a new requirement with a user-provided id= parameter, should the script verify that the ID follows the sequential pattern (i.e., is exactly next-highest ID), or just check that it's not a duplicate?

options.label: Only check for duplicates - allow any non-duplicate ID that matches the format
options.pros: Maximum flexibility, allows fixing gaps in sequences, permits custom ID schemes for special cases
options.cons: Could create non-sequential IDs, harder to track next ID, violates the sequential numeric format intention

options.label: Enforce strict sequentiality - only allow the next expected ID in sequence
options.pros: Maintains strict sequence integrity, prevents gaps, easier to understand and manage, aligns with auto-generation logic
options.cons: Less flexible, cannot fix existing gaps or reuse deleted IDs, might block legitimate use cases

options.label: Warn on non-sequential IDs but allow them - print warning to stderr if ID breaks sequence
options.pros: Flexible yet protective, alerts user to potential issues, allows override for special cases
options.cons: Warning might be ignored, could still lead to sequence fragmentation, middle-ground solution

questions.recommendation-rationale: The prompt states 'Automatically generate IDs unless id= parameter is provided' and describes ID generation as 'scanning the requirements file to find the highest existing ID in each category and incrementing by 1'. This implies strict sequentiality is the design intent. Enforcing strict sequentiality maintains data integrity and prevents sequence fragmentation. Users who need to override can use validation=none if implemented.

user-selection.value: Abandon the requirement to exist parameter "user-provided id= parameter". Always the script decides what should be the next ID. This overwrites the prompt requirement.

questions.question-text: Should the 'strict' validation mode check for duplicated requirement text (i.e., same description already exists), or only validate format and content quality?

options.label: Check for text duplicates - fail if identical requirement text already exists
options.pros: Prevents accidental duplication, improves requirement quality, catches copy-paste errors
options.cons: Might block legitimate similar requirements, requires fuzzy matching logic, performance overhead

options.label: Only validate format and content quality - no duplicate text checking
options.pros: Simpler implementation, allows intentionally similar requirements, better performance
options.cons: Won't catch duplicate requirements, user must manually check for duplicates

options.label: Check for exact text duplicates only - fail on 100% identical text
options.pros: Catches obvious copy-paste errors, simple exact-match logic, minimal performance impact
options.cons: Won't catch near-duplicates, two requirements could be 99% identical and still pass

questions.recommendation-rationale: Exact duplicate checking provides good value with minimal complexity. It catches obvious mistakes (copy-paste errors) without the complexity and false positives of fuzzy matching. This aligns with 'enhanced checks' intent of strict mode while staying focused on format compliance.

user-selection.value: Strict validation is abandoned. This overwrites the prompt requirement.

questions.question-text: When updating execution instructions, should we add inline warnings within the execution flow, or consolidate warnings into a dedicated 'Safety Rules' section?

options.label: Inline warnings - add warnings at each point where requirements might be edited
options.pros: Warnings are context-specific and visible exactly when needed, harder to miss, reinforces message through repetition
options.cons: Can make instructions verbose, multiple similar warnings might clutter the document

options.label: Consolidated section - add a single 'Safety Rules' or 'Requirements Management' section at the top
options.pros: Clean organization, single source of truth, easy to reference, keeps instructions concise
options.cons: Might be skipped if user jumps to specific steps, less visible in context

options.label: Both - add a prominent section plus brief inline reminders
options.pros: Best of both worlds, comprehensive coverage, redundancy ensures visibility
options.cons: Most verbose approach, potential for inconsistency between section and inline warnings

questions.recommendation-rationale: The prompt states 'Add prominent warning: NEVER edit requirements.md directly - always use scripts'. The word 'prominent' suggests high visibility is crucial. Combining a dedicated section (for comprehensive rules) with brief inline reminders (at critical points) ensures the message is never missed while maintaining good document structure.

questions.question-text: How should the scripts handle atomic writes - use a simple temp file approach, or implement full transactional safety with backup/rollback capability?

options.label: Simple temp file - write to temp, then rename (standard atomic write pattern)
options.pros: Simple, reliable, OS-level atomicity guarantees, matches standard practice
options.cons: No rollback if later validation fails, no backup created, lost original on corruption

options.label: Full transactional - create backup, write to temp, validate, then commit with option to rollback
options.pros: Complete safety, can recover from any failure, backup available for manual recovery
options.cons: More complex implementation, requires cleanup of old backups, potential disk space usage

options.label: Simple temp + backup copy - create timestamped backup before any changes, then use temp file approach
options.pros: Good safety balance, simple implementation, backup available if something goes wrong
options.cons: Backup not automatically rolled back, requires manual intervention if issues occur

questions.recommendation-rationale: The prompt states 'Use atomic writes (temp file + rename) to prevent corruption'. This explicitly describes the simple temp file approach. The framework follows the 'fail fast before making any file modifications' principle, validating everything before writing. Combined with atomic writes, this provides adequate safety without over-engineering. Requirement UR-0028 ('destructive operations shall create backups') doesn't classify requirement modifications as destructive operations.
